cards.front: After var list = new ArrayList<>();, can you add a String and an Integer to it?
cards.back: Yes — it is an ArrayList<Object>, so any reference type fits; adding values never changes the inferred type
cards.extra: Autoboxing turns 123 into Integer and true into Boolean. The variable's type was fixed at its declaration from the standalone initializer, so mixed elements do not narrow it to ArrayList<String> — that assignment still fails with incompatible types. This is the loss of generic type safety the diamond-with-var trap causes.
cards.example:
var list = new ArrayList<>();
list.add("x");
list.add(123);
list.add(true);   // ok: [x, 123, true]

cards.back: List<String> — the factory's type arguments come from the actual arguments, so no target type is needed
cards.extra: Unlike new ArrayList<>(), List.of(...) and Map.of(...) have real values to infer from: Map.of("a", 1) gives Map<String, Integer>. With var this is the convenient way to get a correctly typed, immutable collection; use new ArrayList<>(List.of(...)) if you need mutability.
cards.example:
var list = List.of("a", "b");
List<String> typed = list;      // ok
var map = Map.of("a", 1);  // Map<String,Integer>
